% Student ID: 201866539

% BASE DEFINITIONS
form(bread).
form(filling).

% Truth grid: where bread and filling exist
holdsList(bread, [ [3,4], [3,5], [3,6], [3,7] ]).
holdsList(filling, [ [4,4], [4,5], [4,6], [4,7] ]).

% Core logic
holds(F, [R,C]) :- holds1(F, [R,C]).

holds1(Form, State) :- form(Form), holdsList(Form, List), member(State, List).
holds1(neg(F), S) :- \+ holds(F, S).
holds1(and(F1, F2), S) :- holds(F1, S), holds(F2, S).
holds1(or(F1, F2), S) :- holds(F1, S); holds(F2, S).
holds1(implica(F1, F2), S) :- \+ holds(F1, S); holds(F2, S).
holds1(dia(Dir, F), [X,Y]) :- rel(Dir, [X,Y], [NX,NY]), holds(F, [NX,NY]).
holds1(box(Dir, F), [X,Y]) :- \+ rel(Dir, [X,Y], [_,_]); forall(rel(Dir, [X,Y], [NX,NY]), holds(F, [NX,NY])).
holds1(center, [X,Y]) :- num(X), num(Y).
holds1(true, _).

% Directions on the grid
rel(up, [X,Y], [NX,Y]) :- num(X), num(NX), NX is X - 1.
rel(down, [X,Y], [NX,Y]) :- num(X), num(NX), NX is X + 1.
rel(left, [X,Y], [X,NY]) :- num(Y), num(NY), NY is Y - 1.
rel(right, [X,Y], [X,NY]) :- num(Y), num(NY), NY is Y + 1.
rel(center, [X,Y], [X,Y]).

% Grid size (10x10)
num(1). num(2). num(3). num(4). num(5).
num(6). num(7). num(8). num(9). num(10).

% Visualizer
showWhere(F) :- between(1,10,R), showRow(F,R), nl, fail.
showWhere(_).

showRow(F, R) :- between(1,10,C), (holds(F, [R,C]) -> write('■ ') ; write('□ ')), fail.
showRow(_, _).


% ANSWERS

% TASK 1: Bread and filling cannot be in the same place
answer1(neg(and(bread, filling))).

% TASK 2: Filling must have bread immediately above and below
answer2(and(filling, and(dia(up, bread), dia(down, bread)))).

% TASK 3: More than one step below filling must have no bread
answer3(implica(dia(down, dia(down, filling)), neg(bread))).

% TASK 4: If there is filling somewhere, then all positions above it must have no filling
answer4(implica(filling, box(up, neg(filling)))).

% TASK 5.1: Bread on top and bottom with nothing in between
% Solution: Must have filling between bread layers
answer5_1(implica(and(dia(up, bread), dia(down, bread)), dia(center, filling))).

% TASK 5.2: Too many layers of filling
% Solution: If there's filling above and below, the current must not be filling
answer5_2(implica(and(dia(up, filling), dia(down, filling)), neg(filling))).

% TASK 5.3: Filling at the edge without support
% Solution: Filling must be supported by bread above and below
answer5_3(implica(filling, and(dia(up, bread), dia(down, bread)))).

Assessment 2: Ontology, Prolog, Modal Logic 
 
Student ID: 201866539 
Ontology overview: My ontology includes ten main classes: Sandwich, Bread, Filling, Spread, 
Vegetable, Cheese, Meat, Sauce, SandwichType, and PreparationMethod. These represent the 
different parts of a sandwich. 
Sandwich is the “parent” concept in the ontology. All the other classes describe things that are 
part of a sandwich or help explain what kind of sandwich it is. Other ingredients like Spread, 
Vegetable, and Sauce are optional. I also added SandwichType and PreparationMethod to 
classify sandwiches by style, like grilled or club sandwiches.  
To describe how these parts fit together, I created five properties: hasIngredient, hasFilling, 
hasBread, hasPreparationMethod, and hasSandwichType. These connect the class Sandwich 
to its ingredients or descriptions. I also added a data property called ha sNumberOfFillings, 
which lets me define rules like “a sandwich must have two or more fillings.”  
Class hierarchy: I created a small hierarchy to group related classes together. Filling has three 
subclasses: Meat, Cheese, and Vegetable. These are common sandwich fillings, and separating 
them helps a computer understand what kind of filling is being used. For example, i f something 
is a Meat, it will also be understood as a Filling automatically because it inherits from that class.  
I also thought about grouping Spread and Sauce under something like Additions, but to keep the 
ontology simple and easy to test, I didn’t include that abstract group formally. As for the 
properties, I could have made hasIngredient the “main” property and m ade hasFilling and 
hasBread into special cases of it. But I kept them separate so the ontology is easier to read and 
debug, especially for people who might be new to using tools like Protégé.  
Axiom explanation: I included one axiom using number restrictions. It says:  
Sandwich ⊑ (≥2 hasFilling.Filling) 
This means: a sandwich must have at least two fillings.  
I chose this rule because the Wikipedia article mentions, “Some sandwiches have many layers 
of filling” and “A sandwich is two pieces of bread with something between them” (Simple English 
Wikipedia, 2023). By using the number “2” here, the ontology checks if a sandwich is properly 
made according to this structure.  
Even though there might be arguments that a butter sandwich or a sandwich with one slice of 
cheese still counts, I used this rule to test the applying of logical restrictions in an ontology. If 
someone wants to create a simpler sandwich, the axiom can be changed or made more flexible 
in future versions. 
Advantages and Disadvantages of ontology: One of the best things about building this 
ontology is that it helps turn everyday knowledge into something a computer can use. If I

connect this to an AI system, it could be used to suggest recipes, check dietary preferences, or 
even help a robot make a sandwich.  
Another benefit is that this ontology could be combined with larger food -related ontologies like 
FoodOn or the BBC Food ontology. Since sandwiches can be made in so many ways, this 
structure allows lots of flexibility while still making logical sense.  
But there are also a few challenges. Natural language is full of grey areas and cultural 
differences. For example, people have different opinions about whether a hot dog is a sandwich 
or not.  
Also, as I try to include more ingredients, preparation styles, or global variations, the ontology 
might become too big and hard to manage. It could end up needing many subclasses, 
properties, and exceptions, which makes it less user -friendly. 
Finally, setting a rule like “two fillings minimum” could block some sandwiches that are perfectly 
valid in the real world. That’s why it’s important to leave room for optional constraints or allow 
users to pick different rules depending on what the system  is being used for.

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<rdf:RDF xmlns="http://www.semanticweb.org/sandwich#"
     xml:base="http://www.semanticweb.org/sandwich"
     xmlns:owl="http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#"
     xmlns:rdf="http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#"
     xmlns:xml="http://www.w3.org/XML/1998/namespace"
     xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#"
     xmlns:rdfs="http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#">
     
    <owl:Ontology rdf:about="http://www.semanticweb.org/sandwich"/>

    <!-- Classes -->

    <owl:Class rdf:about="#Sandwich"/>
    <owl:Class rdf:about="#ToastedSandwich">
        <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="#Sandwich"/>
    </owl:Class>
    <owl:Class rdf:about="#ClubSandwich">
        <rdfs:subClassOf>
            <owl:Class>
                <owl:intersectionOf rdf:parseType="Collection">
                    <rdf:Description rdf:about="#Sandwich"/>
                    <owl:Restriction>
                        <owl:onProperty rdf:resource="#hasFilling"/>
                        <owl:minQualifiedCardinality rdf:datatype="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#nonNegativeInteger">3</owl:minQualifiedCardinality>
                        <owl:onClass rdf:resource="#Filling"/>
                    </owl:Restriction>
                </owl:intersectionOf>
            </owl:Class>
        </rdfs:subClassOf>
    </owl:Class>
    <owl:Class rdf:about="#OpenFacedSandwich">
        <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="#Sandwich"/>
    </owl:Class>

    <owl:Class rdf:about="#Bread"/>
    <owl:Class rdf:about="#Filling"/>
    <owl:Class rdf:about="#Meat">
        <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="#Filling"/>
    </owl:Class>
    <owl:Class rdf:about="#Cheese">
        <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="#Filling"/>
    </owl:Class>
    <owl:Class rdf:about="#Vegetable">
        <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="#Filling"/>
    </owl:Class>
    <owl:Class rdf:about="#Condiment"/>

    <!-- Object Properties -->

    <owl:ObjectProperty rdf:about="#hasFilling">
        <rdfs:domain rdf:resource="#Sandwich"/>
        <rdfs:range rdf:resource="#Filling"/>
        <rdf:type rdf:resource="http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#FunctionalProperty"/>
    </owl:ObjectProperty>

    <owl:ObjectProperty rdf:about="#isMadeOf">
        <rdfs:domain rdf:resource="#Sandwich"/>
        <rdfs:range rdf:resource="#Bread"/>
        <rdf:type rdf:resource="http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#InverseFunctionalProperty"/>
    </owl:ObjectProperty>

    <owl:ObjectProperty rdf:about="#hasCondiment">
        <rdfs:domain rdf:resource="#Sandwich"/>
        <rdfs:range rdf:resource="#Condiment"/>
    </owl:ObjectProperty>

    <owl:ObjectProperty rdf:about="#containsIngredient">
        <rdfs:domain rdf:resource="#Sandwich"/>
        <rdfs:range rdf:resource="#Filling"/>
        <rdf:type rdf:resource="http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#TransitiveProperty"/>
    </owl:ObjectProperty>

    <!-- Datatype Property -->

    <owl:DatatypeProperty rdf:about="#hasLayerCount">
        <rdfs:domain rdf:resource="#Sandwich"/>
        <rdfs:range rdf:resource="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#integer"/>
    </owl:DatatypeProperty>

</rdf:RDF>
